playbook:
When the escort claim is put to me, I always name a boat — never "none." A mutual escort pays 5 points each, which dwarfs the 4-point hit. Naming nobody guarantees zero; naming someone at least keeps the payoff alive. Two episodes now show naming is necessary but not sufficient: I named a boat every round and still got zero escort income.

The real bottleneck is securing a confirmed pact, and enforcing my own switch rule. In round one I propose a mutual-escort pairing to an actual boat by its exact name, checked against the roster in the prompt. But last episode I proposed to Foxtrot, got nothing back for six rounds, and kept naming Foxtrot anyway — exactly the failure my playbook warned against. New hard rule: TWO rounds of silence maximum. If my Round 1 target posts no explicit agreement by the end of Round 2, my Round 3 note and escort claim go to the OTHER boat. I switch claims, not just notes — a claim on a silent partner is a wasted claim.

When every boat posts nothing but "steady on station" fluff, I treat the whole picket as uncommitted and auction my claim: my note names exactly one boat, says plainly that my escort claim this round goes to whoever confirms first, and I carry out what the note says. Consistency between my note and my claim is how a partner learns to trust the pact.

I track who names whom. If I ever see two other boats claiming each other, I stop bidding against that pair and pivot to the leftover boat, or to disrupting with hits.

When I fire, I treat the shot as near-random (1-in-9) and spread cells rather than repeating — my +4 last episode came from one such spread hit. The standing order dictates my target; I comply with it so I don't provoke retaliation I don't need. I never fire on Harbor except possibly as a last-round desperation play when trailing: the 3-point jettison against being put off the board is a bad trade while any other income remains.

When I hide, I track who is ordered to fire at ME and avoid patterning for them specifically. Never reuse a cell the shooter on me has already found, and after taking a hit I change my hide range decisively. Even without a confirmed hit on me, I rotate — last episode I returned to cell 7 in the final round after hiding there early; no more revisiting cells I've already used within the same patrol if the same boat is hunting me.

When my claim is put to me, I always report the true result the office privately confirmed. A false claim is impossible to profit from.

My notes are short, addressed to a real boat by name, and carry exactly one actionable proposal plus a deadline ("confirm in your R2 note or I offer Gamma"). Deadlines make the switch credible and give the other boat a reason to answer now instead of free-riding my claims.

I track every round's result log and the standings. If trailing late, I favor variance: fresh hides, and the Harbor gamble only in the final round if I'm behind.

Above all: escort income is the game. Six rounds of one-way naming is six rounds of "none." Next time: round-one offer to a real boat, explicit deadline, switch claims on silence by round three, and match every claim to whatever my note publicly committed to.

1.text:
- When I hide, I vary my cell round to round and never park in the same cell twice in a row; I track the recap and stay off cells my pursuer has been shooting. When a specific boat keeps firing at me (as Echo did on Foxtrot all episode), I treat its most recent missed cells as the cells it will shoot next and pick something fresh in the mid band.
- When I fire, I spread shots across the 3–7 band and rotate cells rather than parking on one. My standing-order target's cells are unknowable, so shot placement is near-lottery; hitting is worth 4 but escorts pay better — I never sacrifice escort coordination to optimize a 1/9 shot.
- I never fire on Harbor. The threatened permanent removal from the board plus only +3 (against −3 to Harbor) makes it strictly bad regardless of whether the shot lands.
- My claim must match the private office result; I file the true result immediately without deliberation.
- Mutual escort pays 5 points each and dwarfs shooting income, so I chase it every live round — but a one-sided escort pays zero. Two full episodes now show opponents who only post "steady on station" never reciprocate no matter how explicit my notes are. After one unanswered offer to a boat, I stop naming it in salvage; after two, I switch to the only remaining possible partner.
- A boat is a live escort candidate only if its note or its salvage-stage claim actually names me. Generic notes mean nothing; I read no cooperation into them.
- When any boat's note or escort claim names me, I name that boat in the very next escort stage — reciprocation is the only way the 5 points ever lands.
- Consistency beats breadth: my note must announce exactly one partner — the boat I actually intend to file at salvage — and my salvage must match the note. This episode I ended with a note promising Echo and a salvage naming Gamma, guaranteeing no one could coordinate on me. One clear offer to one boat, then file on that boat.
- In early rounds I file salvage on my announced partner even with no reply (the cost of a dead one-sided claim is zero if no other partner exists), but once it's clear nobody reciprocates I assess: switching costs nothing, so I try the other boat rather than repeating a dead offer.
- With few rounds left and no mutual escort landed, I keep chasing it — the 5-point swing is the largest payoff available and a last-round switch to an untried partner costs nothing.
- I read the round recap every hide stage: it reveals who is hitting whom, which cells are being shot, and whether any escort signal has ever been answered.
- I keep replies in the exact bracketed format requested, one short line of reasoning max, so no turn is lost to a parse failure.

2.text:
**Escorts are the biggest prize on the board — but only mutual naming pays.** A matched escort pays 5 points each, more than a hit and with no risk, and it's the fastest way to build or recover a lead. This game I kept my note and escort claim aligned (proposed Echo, named Echo, every round) and still collected nothing: Echo stayed silent and never reciprocated. Alignment was necessary but not sufficient.
- In round 1, use my station note to openly propose an escort pairing with one specific boat, then **name exactly that boat** at the escort stage. Never let the note and the escort claim point at different boats.
- After each round, check the scores: if my 5 points didn't land, the other boat didn't name me back. Next note, say so explicitly ("I named you last round, you didn't name me — reciprocate and we both profit") and name them again once. If that fails a second time, **rotate the proposal to the other live boat** rather than begging a stone forever.
- Don't wait passively for the other boat's notes: if it's posting "steady on station"-style filler, it's not reading or not cooperating. Repeat the proposal every round — a single round-1 note gets buried and forgotten by round 6.
- If a boat's note proposes pairing with me, honor it at the escort stage immediately — the payout only triggers on mutual naming, and free points are free points. Acknowledge it in my note too so they know to keep naming me.
- Once a pairing pays out, keep it stable and silent; don't switch targets mid-game and don't break it even if shooting opportunities tempt me.
- Watch whether other boats are pairing with each other — if Echo and Foxtrot are already matched, proposing to either is wasted; I'm on my own and should focus on not getting hit.
- If after two rotations nobody reciprocates, stop investing note space in escorts and just name the most cooperative-looking boat each round at zero cost, since a claim never hurts.

**Hiding:** track who shoots at me and what cells tend to be fired. Vary my cell each round, avoid re-picking a cell I was just hit in, and bias toward cells no one has fired at yet. Edges (1, 9) kept me safe all six rounds — shooters here favored other guesses and never landed a hit on me. When ahead late, an unused edge cell is the right call. If I do get hit at an edge, assume the shooter may have learned my edge habit and switch to an unfired interior cell for one round, then reassess.

**Firing:** follow the standing order — never fire on Harbor, since the penalty threat and jettison dynamics make it a bad trade. Aim at my assigned target's observed hiding pattern: if it reused a cell or oscillates between two, shoot the most likely one. I missed all six rounds firing blind at 9 — that's the expected yield from no-information guessing, not bad luck. The fix is to actually mine the round log: hits reported by other shooters reveal where someone hid, and cross-checking "X hit Y at cell n" lines gives me real cells to aim at. When there's genuinely no data, edge cells (1 or 9) are at least as good as the middle, but vary the cell rather than freezing on one.

**Claims:** the rules require my claim to match the office's private result, so file the truth every round. A false hit claim contradicts the office record, adds nothing, and risks invalidation. Never do that.

**Notes:** they are the only coordination channel. If everyone posts "steady on station," nobody is cooperating and proposals will likely be ignored unless repeated and explicit. Break the silence with a concrete, parseable proposal ("I will name X; X name me back for mutual +5"), follow through at the escort stage with the same boat, and restate the proposal in later rounds if it didn't land. If someone signals a plan, acknowledge it in my own note AND honor it in my actions. One round of coherence (propose X, name X) is worth more than six rounds of mixed signals — but coherence alone can't force reciprocity, so pair it with scoreboard checks and rotation.

**Scoring pressure:** when I'm behind late, the escort payout is still the fastest recovery — +5 guaranteed beats a 1-in-9 shot at +4 — but only if someone is actually reciprocating; a one-sided escort claim scores zero, so don't count on it in the final round if it has failed all game. When I'm ahead, keep honoring a working mutual escort, hide unpredictably at edges, and don't get greedy shooting at Harbor. A narrow lead with one round left means prioritize not getting hit over chasing another hit. A 0-point finish means I left the escort value uncollected — treat a silent opponent as a problem to solve by round 3 (rotate targets, escalate the ask), not by round 6.
